templates.pattern: A machine does [W] J of work in [T] seconds. Calculate the power output of the machine in watts.
templates.explanation:
Power = Work Done ÷ Time
= [W] ÷ [T]
= [RESULT] W

Power is the rate of doing work. 1 watt = 1 joule per second. A more powerful machine does the same work in less time.

templates.pattern: An electric heater has a power rating of [P] W and is switched on for [T] seconds. Calculate the energy transferred by the heater in joules.
templates.explanation:
Energy = Power × Time
= [P] × [T]
= [RESULT] J

Energy transferred depends on both the power rating and the time the device is used.

templates.pattern: A device transfers [EU] J of useful energy from a total input of [ET] J. Calculate the efficiency of the device as a percentage.
templates.explanation:
Efficiency = (Useful Energy Output ÷ Total Energy Input) × 100
= ([EU] ÷ [ET]) × 100
= [RESULT]%

No device is 100% efficient. Energy is always lost to the surroundings, usually as heat.

templates.pattern: A crate of mass [M] kg is lifted vertically through a height of [H] m. Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy of the crate in joules. (g = 10 m/s²)
templates.explanation:
Gravitational Potential Energy = mass × g × height
= [M] × 10 × [H]
= [RESULT] J

GPE is stored energy due to position in a gravitational field. The higher the object and the greater its mass, the more GPE it has.

templates.pattern: A car of mass [M] kg is moving at a velocity of [V] m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy of the car in joules.
templates.explanation:
Kinetic Energy = ½ × mass × velocity²
= 0.5 × [M] × [V]²
= 0.5 × [M] × [V*V]
= [RESULT] J

Doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy. This is why speed is so important in road safety.

templates.pattern: A [P] W appliance is used for [T] hours. Calculate the energy consumed in kilowatt-hours (kWh).
templates.explanation:
Energy (kWh) = Power (kW) × Time (h)
= ([P] ÷ 1000) × [T]
= [P/1000] × [T]
= [RESULT] kWh

Electricity bills are calculated using kilowatt-hours. 1 kWh is the energy used by a 1000 W device running for 1 hour.

templates.pattern: An object of mass [M] kg is dropped from a height of [H] m. Assuming no energy losses, calculate the speed of the object just before it hits the ground in m/s. (g = 10 m/s²)
templates.explanation:
Using conservation of energy: GPE = KE
mgh = ½mv²
v = √(2gh)
= √(2 × 10 × [H])
= √[2*10*H]
= [RESULT] m/s

Mass cancels out — the speed does not depend on the mass of the object.

templates.pattern: A machine has a useful power output of [P] W and an efficiency of [EFF]%. Calculate the total power input to the machine in watts.
templates.explanation:
Efficiency = (Power Output ÷ Power Input) × 100
Rearranging: Power Input = Power Output × 100 ÷ Efficiency
= [P] × 100 ÷ [EFF]
= [RESULT] W

A less efficient machine requires more power input to produce the same useful output.

templates.pattern: A [P] W light bulb operates at [EFF]% efficiency for [T] seconds. Calculate the energy wasted as heat in joules.
templates.explanation:
Total energy input = P × t = [P] × [T] = [P*T] J
Wasted energy = Total energy × (1 − efficiency)
= [P*T] × (1 − [EFF]/100)
= [P*T] × [1-EFF/100]
= [RESULT] J

The rest of the energy ([EFF]%) is transferred as useful light energy.

templates.pattern: A crane lifts a load of mass [M] kg through a vertical height of [H] m in [T] seconds. Calculate the useful power output of the crane in watts. (g = 10 m/s²)
templates.explanation:
Useful Power = Work Done ÷ Time
= (mass × g × height) ÷ time
= ([M] × 10 × [H]) ÷ [T]
= [M*10*H] ÷ [T]
= [RESULT] W

This is the minimum power needed — a real crane would need more due to inefficiency.
